thread.title: Apple CEO Tim Cook has some harsh words for Facebook

title: Apple CEO Tim Cook has some harsh words for Facebook
text:
When Apple Inc. Chief Executive Tim Cook was asked how he’d handle the Facebook Inc./Cambridge Analytica scandal, his answer spoke volumes about how he really felt about the situation.
“I wouldn’t be in this situation,” Cook said at a Recode/MSNBC taping Wednesday. 
He contrasted Facebook’s FB, +0.53% strategy of monetizing consumers with Apple’s AAPL, -1.10% strategy of selling hardware to consumers. 
“The truth is, we could make a ton of money if we monetized our consumer, if our consumer was our product,” Cook said, according to Recode. “We’ve elected not to do that.”
Apple is able to monetize its user base through its services segment, though that mainly consists of getting iPhone users to buy things like Apple Music subscriptions, in-app purchases, and iCloud storage. The company doesn’t sell consumer data to marketers, which is the distinction. The bulk of Apple’s revenue still comes from hardware sales.
Don’t miss: Three ways Apple could spend $163 billion besides a big acquisition 
Cook said that while he thinks “the best regulation is no regulation, is self-regulation,” he also thought that Facebook was “beyond” that point now.
At the taping, Cook also spent time defending Apple’s manufacturing practices, saying that he believes iPhones are made in the U.S. because some of their parts are made here, even though the devices are ultimately assembled overseas in China. 
“It’s not true that iPhone isn’t built in the United States,” he said. He explained that glass for the iPhone comes from Kentucky, while lasers that enable facial recognition are made in Texas. 
Cook refers to Corning Inc. GLW, -1.41% and Finisar Corp. FNSR, -3.95% which are thus far the two recipients of awards from Apple’s Manufacturing Fund, through which the company has committed to awarding $5 billion to U.S. businesses. These awards help Apple as well, in better ensuring that suppliers can provide Apple enough of certain components as it ramps up device production.
See also: Why the Facebook controversy could be good for Apple 
The assembly of iPhones in China has become a political issue during the Trump presidency, with Trump having said last summer that Cook promised to build three U.S. plants . At the start of this year, Apple announced plans to “contribute” $350 billion to the U.S. economy over five years, through investments in U.S. companies as well as the creation of 20,000 jobs. Apple didn’t specify how many of those jobs would be full-time positions at Apple. 
Cook said at the Recode event that the company didn’t need political pressure to create jobs in the U.S. because the company was already doing so. 
“We love this country. We’re patriots. This is our country. Want to create as many jobs in the U.S. as we can,” he said. 
Apple’s patriotism has been called into question in the past, including in late 2015 when the company fought government requests to unlock the iPhone belonging to the San Bernardino shooter. 
“Customers expect Apple and other technology companies to do everything in our power to protect their personal information, and at Apple we are deeply committed to safeguarding their data,” Apple said at the time, words that take on new relevance in light of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. One analyst has floated the possibility that Apple could benefit from the scrutiny over Facebook , as Apple doesn’t monetize user data. 
Apple shares are down 0.4% in Wednesday trading but up 17% over the past 12 months. Facebook shares are up 8.6% the past year, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, -0.04% of which Apple is a component, is up 16% in that time.
